challenges.title: Database Schema Design: Tables, Keys, and Constraints
description: Good database design is the foundation of scalable applications. In PostgreSQL, you define schemas — the structure of your tables — using CREATE TABLE with typed columns and constraints.

-- PostgreSQL schema example CREATE TABLE users ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, -- auto-increment integer email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, role VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'user', created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW() ); CREATE TABLE posts ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, user_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, title TEXT NOT NULL, content TEXT, published BOOLEAN DEFAULT false ); -- Index for fast lookups CREATE INDEX idx_posts_user_id ON posts(user_id); CREATE INDEX idx_posts_published ON posts(published) WHERE published = true;
Key constraints: PRIMARY KEY (unique identifier), FOREIGN KEY (referential integrity), UNIQUE (no duplicates), NOT NULL (required field), CHECK (custom validation), DEFAULT (fallback value).
Indexes dramatically speed up queries but slow down writes — add them on columns you frequently filter, sort, or join on.

Write a function validateSchema that takes a table definition object { columns: [{name, type, required, unique}] } and a data row object, and returns an array of validation error strings. Return an empty array if the row is valid.
challengeSeed: // Collect error messages for each violation
tests: var schema = {columns:[{name:'email',type:'string',required:true},{name:'age',type:'number',required:false}]}; var r1 = validateSchema(schema, {email:'a@b.com',age:25}); assert(r1.length === 0, 'message: Valid row should return no errors.');
var r2 = validateSchema(schema, {age:25}); assert(r2.length === 1 && r2[0] === 'email is required', 'message: Missing required field should produce an error.');
var r3 = validateSchema(schema, {email:'a@b.com', age:'not a number'}); assert(r3.length === 1 && r3[0].includes('number'), 'message: Wrong type should produce a type error.');

challenges.title: Transactions: ACID Guarantees
description: Database transactions group multiple operations into a single atomic unit — either all operations succeed, or none do. This is the foundation of data integrity.

-- PostgreSQL transaction BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2; -- Both succeed COMMIT; -- Or if something fails: ROLLBACK; -- undo everything

Transactions guarantee ACID properties: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (valid state before and after), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes).
In 2026, understanding transactions is critical for: payment processing, inventory management, multi-step user registration flows, and any operation where partial failure would corrupt data.

Implement a simple createTransaction function that simulates database transaction behavior. It takes an initial state object and returns an object with update(key, value), commit() (returns new state), and rollback() (discards changes, returns original state).
challengeSeed: // Make current changes permanent, return new state
tests: var tx = createTransaction({balance: 1000}); tx.update('balance', 500); assert(tx.commit().balance === 500, 'message: commit() should persist the update.');
var tx2 = createTransaction({balance: 1000}); tx2.update('balance', 500); assert(tx2.rollback().balance === 1000, 'message: rollback() should restore original state.');
var tx3 = createTransaction({a:1}); tx3.update('a', 99); tx3.rollback(); tx3.update('a', 42); assert(tx3.commit().a === 42, 'message: Should be able to update after rollback.');
